knowledgeChecks.title: Knowledge check: KYC and AML foundations

questions.prompt: What is a sound first response when an assigned KYC task has an unresolved evidence gap?

choices.text: Fill the gap using the most likely explanation.
Record what is missing and route it through the approved process.
Ignore it if the customer seems trustworthy.
Ask a colleague to approve it in a personal chat.

questions.explanation: An unresolved gap should be described factually and sent to the designated reviewer or workflow. Learners should not guess or bypass controls.

questions.prompt: Which statement is an observation rather than an allegation?

choices.text: The customer is laundering money.
The customer is dishonest.
The sample file contains no invoice for the listed transfers.
The account should be rejected.

questions.explanation: A source-based statement about what the file contains is an observation. Intent or disposition requires evidence and an authorized decision.

questions.prompt: A company application includes a representative's signed form. What should the operations learner establish?

choices.text: That the representative is popular with the directors.
That the person has authority under accepted evidence and the approved workflow.
That the signature looks familiar.
That the customer has no beneficial owners.

questions.explanation: Authority is a separate check. Follow the accepted evidence and procedure; a signature by itself does not settle authority.

questions.prompt: An ownership chart stops at an unnamed holding company. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Assume the directors own the holding company.
Close the case because an entity was named.
Record the incomplete chain and request clarification through the approved checklist.
Mark all shareholders as high risk.

questions.explanation: The ownership/control chain remains unresolved. Document the gap and use the legal-entity workflow to obtain or escalate the required information.

knowledgeChecks.title: Knowledge check: risk and ongoing review

questions.prompt: What does a higher-risk classification mean in an approved risk framework?

choices.text: The customer has committed a crime.
Apply the relevant controls and approvals; it is not proof of wrongdoing.
Stop documenting the case.
Use a personal scoring method.

questions.explanation: Risk classifications guide due diligence and approval controls. They are not findings of guilt.

questions.prompt: A dated regulatory notice describes a time-limited measure. Before using it in current work, what should staff do?

choices.text: Apply it permanently because it was once official.
Check the latest official text, conditions, and the institution's current procedure.
Ignore all official notices.
Apply it to every type of customer.

questions.explanation: Dated provisions can expire or have narrow scope. Verify the current official text and internal guidance before relying on them.

knowledgeChecks.title: Knowledge check: screening and transaction review

questions.prompt: A screening tool returns a similar name but a different date-of-birth field. What should the learner conclude?

choices.text: The match is confirmed.
The result is a prompt for review; compare approved identifiers and escalate uncertainty.
The person is suspicious.
Delete the alert.

questions.explanation: A name similarity does not establish identity. Preserve the result, compare permitted information, and follow the match-review process.

questions.prompt: A transaction alert by itself establishes that a customer intended to launder money.

choices.text: True
False; the alert initiates a review and is not a conclusion about intent.
True only if a transaction is large.
True if there is no invoice in one sample file.

questions.explanation: An alert is a review trigger. Staff must document facts and context without making unsupported allegations.

knowledgeChecks.title: Knowledge check: case documentation and safe handling

questions.prompt: Which elements make a useful case handoff?

choices.text: An unsupported label and a suggested customer punishment.
Trigger, dates, sources reviewed, facts, open questions, actions, and next owner.
Only the learner's final conclusion.
A screenshot sent through a personal messaging account.

questions.explanation: A reviewer needs a reproducible factual trail and clear next action. Keep the handoff in approved systems.

questions.prompt: A colleague requests a real customer document in an unapproved class chat. What should you do?

choices.text: Share it after hiding the account number.
Refuse to share, use fictional learning data, and follow the approved privacy/security route if it was already posted.
Copy it into a public AI tool to summarize it.
Forward it to a personal email address.

questions.explanation: Customer information belongs only in approved work systems and authorized tasks. Learning activities should use fictional records.

finalAssessment.title: KYC & AML Operations Foundations — final assessment

questions.prompt: Which outcome best describes the purpose of KYC controls?

choices.text: Understand the customer and relationship using required identification and due-diligence steps.
Guarantee that a customer will never present risk.
Replace all institutional procedures with personal judgement.
Collect as much personal information as possible.

questions.explanation: KYC supports customer understanding and required controls; it cannot guarantee zero risk and should follow applicable rules and policy.

questions.prompt: Which action is within an entry-level learner's safe role when a case is uncertain?

choices.text: Approve the case to avoid delay.
Make a final suspicious-activity finding.
Record evidence and route the open issue to the designated reviewer.
Tell the customer an internal alert was raised.

questions.explanation: The learner follows assigned procedures, preserves evidence, and escalates uncertainty without exceeding authority.

questions.prompt: A system output is relevant to a customer check. What should the case note include?

choices.text: Only the learner's opinion.
The approved source or check, date, result, and unresolved difference.
A guess about why the data differs.
No note if the result was unexpected.

questions.explanation: Source, date, result, and open issue make the work traceable and reproducible.

questions.prompt: For a company account, what is the correct approach to the person's authority to act?

choices.text: Assume any employee who submits a form is authorized.
Check accepted authority evidence using the institution's approved workflow.
Use the person's job title alone in every case.
Skip authority if identity was verified.

questions.explanation: Identity and authority are distinct. Follow the accepted records and procedure for the entity and task.

questions.prompt: A beneficial-ownership chain is incomplete. Which note is most appropriate?

choices.text: The customer is hiding ownership.
The chart ends at an unnamed holding company; required ownership information remains unresolved and is routed for review.
The directors are the beneficial owners by default.
No issue exists because a chart was supplied.

questions.explanation: State the observable gap and next action. Do not infer intent or ownership.

questions.prompt: Which statement about customer identification is correct?

choices.text: Every customer type always uses the same checklist.
Use the procedure for the relevant customer type, product, and relationship.
A readable copy is automatically verified.
Extra data should be collected just in case.

questions.explanation: The applicable steps vary by customer and relationship; verification must use permitted methods and data minimization.

questions.prompt: How should an operations learner use an approved risk classification?

choices.text: As proof of guilt.
As a guide to prescribed controls, evidence, and approval levels.
As a replacement for documentation.
As a personal label based on a customer's background.

questions.explanation: Risk informs the proportional control process; it is not proof and must not rely on stereotypes.

questions.prompt: A customer's activity changes from the stated profile. What is the appropriate response?

choices.text: Assume criminal intent.
Compare activity with current information, preserve relevant facts, and follow the review workflow.
Ignore it if the customer is long-standing.
Ask the customer whether they are laundering money.

questions.explanation: Ongoing review compares activity with what is known, records evidence, and routes open questions through policy.

questions.prompt: A legal or regulatory notice contains a dated allowance. What must be checked before relying on it?

choices.text: Whether it was once mentioned in training.
Its current validity, effective date, conditions, scope, and current institutional procedure.
Nothing; official notices never expire.
Whether another bank used it.

questions.explanation: Dated provisions can expire or be limited. Confirm the current official text and scope.

questions.prompt: A screening result has a similar name but a conflicting permitted identifier. What is the right next step?

choices.text: Confirm the match from the name alone.
Record similarities and differences and route uncertainty to the authorized reviewer.
Delete the result.
Notify the customer of the possible match.

questions.explanation: Name similarity alone does not establish identity. Follow the approved review and confidentiality procedures.

questions.prompt: What does a transaction-monitoring alert mean?

choices.text: The customer has committed a crime.
Activity has been flagged for review against context and policy.
A report has automatically been filed.
The account must always be closed.

questions.explanation: An alert is a prompt to review, not a conclusion, filing decision, or automatic disposition.

questions.prompt: Which case-note sentence is most objective?

choices.text: The customer is obviously fraudulent.
Three incoming transfers from a new counterparty appear in the sample alert; no matching invoice was present in the records reviewed.
The customer probably lied about the business.
Nothing can be trusted.

questions.explanation: This sentence states observable activity and the scope of the record review without assigning intent.

questions.prompt: Where should real customer information be used for assigned case work?

choices.text: Any convenient messaging tool.
Only approved systems, for an authorized task, with necessary access.
A public AI assistant if identifiers are partially masked.
A personal device note app.

questions.explanation: Limit access to approved work systems and authorized tasks. Training examples should be fictional.

questions.prompt: A learner notices an internal review detail in a group chat. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Forward it so others can decide.
Avoid further sharing and follow the approved privacy/security reporting route.
Tell the customer immediately.
Copy it into a workbook.

questions.explanation: Protect confidentiality, stop unnecessary disclosure, and use the designated internal route.

questions.prompt: Who makes any required suspicious-transaction reporting decision?

choices.text: Any learner who sees an alert.
The designated officer or authorized role under applicable law and institutional policy.
The customer-facing teller alone.
The course assessment system.

questions.explanation: Reporting decisions are governed by applicable law and institutional policy and belong to authorized roles.
